title: First words
goal: Greet people, say thank you, sorry and goodbye, ask people to repeat or slow down, and count to ten thousand.

notes.h: Two ways to say thank you and sorry
notes.p: {{감사합니다}} and {{죄송합니다}} are the formal versions: the safe choice with strangers, staff and older people. {{고마워요}} and {{미안해요}} are softer and friendlier but still polite. When in doubt, use the formal ones.

notes.h: Goodbye depends on who is leaving
notes.p: Korean has two goodbyes. If the other person is leaving, say {{안녕히 가세요}} (go in peace). If you are leaving and they stay, say {{안녕히 계세요}} (stay in peace). If you both walk off in different directions, use {{안녕히 가세요}}.
ex: Goodbye (when you leave and they stay).

notes.p: Korean has two number systems. Native Korean numbers ({{하나}}, {{둘}}, {{셋}} … {{열}}) are for counting things and people. Sino-Korean numbers ({{일}}, {{이}}, {{삼}} …) are for money, prices, dates and phone numbers, and they build like a calculator: {{십오}} is 10 + 5 and {{이십}} is 2 × 10. Big numbers go in ten-thousands: {{만}} is 10,000, so 15,000 is {{만 오천}}. {{백}}, {{천}} and {{만}} need no 'one' in front. Never mix the two systems inside one number.

{{주세요}} means 'please give me'. Put a thing in front of it to ask for it: {{이거 하나 주세요}} (one of these, please). Put an action in front to ask for a favour: {{말해 주세요}} (please say it), {{천천히 말해 주세요}} (please speak slowly).

Korean is not always said the way it is spelled, and the 'said like' line under each phrase shows the change. A final ㅂ before ㄴ is said as ㅁ, so {{감사합니다}} sounds like {{감사함니다}}. A final consonant slides onto a following vowel, so {{한국어}} sounds like {{한구거}}. In {{여덟}} the final ㄹㅂ is said as just ㄹ.

vocab.en: It's okay / I'm fine / No thanks
vocab.note: Very common. Also a polite way to decline an offer.
Literally "go in peace". Say it when the other person leaves.
Literally "stay in peace". Say it when you leave and they stay.
How you call a server in a restaurant.

vocab.en: I don't know / I don't understand

vocab.note: -아/어 주세요 = "please do … for me".
해요 = do / speak.

vocab.en: Before eating: thank you for the meal
vocab.note: Said before eating, especially when someone else is paying or cooked.

vocab.en: After eating: that was great, thank you
vocab.note: Said after the meal to the host or whoever paid.
Sino-Korean numbers: used for money, minutes, dates, phone numbers.
Korean counts big numbers in ten-thousands: 만 원 = 10,000 won.
Native Korean numbers: used to count things and people, and for the hour. Before a counter word it shortens to 한.
Shortens to 두 before a counter: 두 명 = two people.
Shortens to 세: 세 시 = three o'clock.
Shortens to 네: 네 개 = four items.
The ㄹㅂ at the end is said as just ㄹ.

vocab.en: Please give me … / Please do … for me
vocab.note: Put a thing or an action in front: {{이거 주세요}}, {{말해 주세요}}.
Point and say {{이거 주세요}}: this one, please.
A polite reply to thanks. In everyday talk Koreans also often say {{아니에요}} (not at all).
{{하세요}} is the respectful form of {{해요}}, used when asking about the other person.

vocab.en: Welcome! (said by staff or a host)
vocab.note: You hear it as you walk into shops and restaurants. Just answer {{안녕하세요}}.
A respectful good night, said to someone going to bed.

items.en: Goodbye! (You are leaving a shop; the owner stays.)
items.why: The person leaving says {{안녕히 계세요}} (stay in peace) to the person who stays.

items.en: Goodbye! (A guest is leaving your home.)
items.why: The other person is leaving, so you wish them {{안녕히 가세요}} (go in peace).

items.en: Please speak slowly.
items.why: {{말해 주세요}} = please say it (for me). {{주세요}} turns an action into a polite request.

items.en: I speak a little Korean.
items.why: {{조금}} = a little. {{천천히}} is slowly and {{다시}} is again.

items.en: Thank you for the meal! (said just before you start eating)
items.why: Before eating it is {{잘 먹겠습니다}}; after eating it is {{잘 먹었습니다}}.

items.en: No, I'm fine. (turning down an offer)
items.why: {{괜찮아요}} (it's okay, I'm fine) is the polite way to say no thanks.

items.en: Excuse me, do you speak English?
items.why: {{저기요}} gets a stranger's attention. {{잠깐만요}} means just a moment.

items.en: Do you speak English?
items.why: {{하세요}} is the respectful form of {{해요}} (do, speak). {{계세요}} is stay and {{가세요}} is go.

items.en: One of these, please.
items.why: Counting things uses native numbers, so one is {{하나}}. The short form {{한}} is only used directly before a counter word, and {{일}} is the Sino-Korean one.

items.en: one, two, three, four (Sino-Korean)
items.why: {{일, 이}} are Sino-Korean, so three is {{삼}}. {{셋}} is native.

items.en: one, two, three, four (native Korean)
items.why: {{하나, 둘}} are native numbers, so three is {{셋}}. {{세}} is only the short form before a counter word.

items.en: five, six, seven, eight (native Korean)
items.why: Native seven is {{일곱}}. {{칠}} is the Sino-Korean seven.

items.en: fifteen
items.why: Sino-Korean builds like a calculator: {{십}} (10) + {{오}} (5) = {{십오}}. Native {{다섯}} never mixes with {{십}}.

items.en: twenty thousand
fifteen thousand
items.why: Korean has its own word for 10,000, {{만}}. Fifteen thousand is 'ten-thousand five-thousand': {{만 오천}}. There is no 'ten thousand' built from {{십}} and {{천}}.

items.en: one hundred and twenty
items.why: {{백}} (100) + {{이십}} (2 × 10) = 120. {{십이}} is 12, {{이백}} is 200, and native {{스물}} can't mix with {{백}}.

items.q: You are leaving a small shop. The owner stays behind the counter. You say:
items.why: You are the one leaving, so you tell the owner to stay in peace: {{안녕히 계세요}}.

items.q: A friend has visited your home and is now leaving. You are staying. You say:
items.why: They are leaving, so you wish them {{안녕히 가세요}} (go in peace).

items.q: You bump into an older stranger on the train and want to apologize properly. You say:
items.why: {{죄송합니다}} is the formal apology for a stranger or an older person. {{감사합니다}} is thank you.

items.q: A shop clerk hands you your change. You thank them. You say:
items.why: {{감사합니다}} is the standard thank you to staff. {{천만에요}} is the reply when someone thanks you.

items.q: Your friend's mother has cooked dinner for you, and you are about to start eating. You say:
items.why: Before the meal: {{잘 먹겠습니다}}. {{잘 먹었습니다}} is for when you have finished.

items.q: You are in a restaurant and want to call the server over. You say:
items.why: {{저기요}} is how you call a server or get a stranger's attention.

items.q: Someone thanks you for holding the door. You reply:
items.why: {{천만에요}} = you're welcome.

items.q: A Korean speaker is talking too fast for you. Ask them to slow down. You say:
items.why: {{천천히}} = slowly, and {{말해 주세요}} = please say it.

items.en: Please speak slowly.
Sorry, please say that once more.
items.full: 미안해요, 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.

opts: Goodbye (said by someone who is leaving).
Goodbye (said to someone who is leaving).
Thanks, I enjoyed the meal. (after eating)

turns.why: {{괜찮아요}} (it's okay) is the answer to an apology. {{천만에요}} answers a thank-you.
Answer a welcome with the greeting {{안녕하세요}}. {{안녕히 가세요}} is goodbye, and {{잘 먹었습니다}} is for after the meal.

turns.en: (You point at a dish on the menu.) This one?

turns.why: Counting things uses native {{하나}}. {{한}} is only used directly before a counter word, and {{일}} is Sino-Korean.

turns.en: (After your meal, as you leave) Thank you. Goodbye.

turns.why: After eating, say {{잘 먹었습니다}}. You are the one leaving, so {{안녕히 가세요}} doesn't fit.
You have just arrived, so greet her with {{안녕하세요}}. The other two are goodbye and good night.
You are about to eat: {{잘 먹겠습니다}}.
{{괜찮아요}} politely turns down more food, and you have finished eating, so {{잘 먹었습니다}}.
You are starting a conversation, so greet with {{안녕하세요}}. The other two are goodbyes.

turns.en: Oh, I'm sorry. Do you speak Korean?

opts: 네, 조금 해요. 천천히 말해 주세요.
네, 조금 하세요. 천천히 말해 주세요.
아니요, 조금 해요. 천천히 말해 주세요.
turns.why: Talk about yourself with plain {{해요}}. {{하세요}} shows respect, so it is for asking about the other person. {{아니요}} doesn't fit with speaking a little.
{{하나, 둘}} are native numbers, so the next one is native {{셋}}. {{세}} is only the short form before a counter word.
{{일, 이}} are Sino-Korean, so the next one is {{삼}}.
Thirty is 3 × 10: {{삼십}}. {{십삼}} is thirteen, and native {{셋}} can't mix with {{십}}.

roleplay.title: Hello and goodbye at a shop
roleplay.setup: You walk into a small corner shop in Seoul. Greet the owner, ask for something by pointing, and leave politely.
roleplay.persona: You are a friendly middle-aged shop owner in Seoul. Speak only very simple polite Korean from level 1: 어서 오세요, 안녕하세요, 이거요?, 네, 감사합니다, 괜찮아요, 안녕히 가세요, and numbers. The learner is a complete beginner. If they ask you to slow down or repeat, do it, slowly. When the learner leaves, say 감사합니다. 안녕히 가세요. and expect 안녕히 계세요 back; if they say 안녕히 가세요, gently model 안녕히 계세요.
goals: Point at something and ask for one
Ask the owner to speak slowly or say it again
Say thank you and the right goodbye as you leave

roleplay.title: Numbers with a friend
roleplay.setup: Your friend Junho helps you practise Korean numbers.
roleplay.persona: You are Junho, a patient Korean friend in his 30s. Help a complete beginner practise numbers using very simple polite Korean from level 1. Say a short run of numbers and let them say the next one, or ask them to count. Alternate native numbers (하나 to 열) and Sino-Korean numbers (일 to 십, then tens, 백, 천, 만, e.g. 만 오천). Keep praise short, correct gently, and slow down when asked.
goals: Count from one to ten with native numbers
Count from one to ten with Sino-Korean numbers
Say a big number such as 15,000
Ask Junho to repeat or slow down
